name: Delayed puberty (male)
aliases: constitutional delay of growth and puberty

reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Delay is conventionally defined as absent testicular enlargement (testes remaining below the pre-pubertal volume) by the upper age limit of the normal population
The commonest cause is constitutional delay of growth and puberty, a benign familial variant that ultimately proceeds to full normal maturation
Constitutional delay must be distinguished from permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and from primary testicular (hypergonadotropic) failure
A family history of late puberty, delayed bone age matching height age, and eventual spontaneous progression support a constitutional cause
Low gonadotropins with anosmia suggest Kallmann syndrome, while raised gonadotropins with small firm testes point to primary gonadal failure such as Klinefelter syndrome
Bone age assessment helps estimate remaining growth potential and supports counselling of the adolescent and family

Management ranges from watchful reassurance in constitutional delay to a short supervised course of androgen to induce secondary characteristics, or definitive hormone induction where hypogonadism is confirmed
reference.pathophysiology: Male puberty begins with reactivation of pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion, driving pituitary luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone release and, in turn, testicular testosterone production and spermatogenesis. Delayed puberty results from disturbance at any point along this axis. In constitutional delay the axis is simply reactivated later than average, following a familial timetable, and maturation is ultimately complete. In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism there is deficient central drive, whether congenital, as in Kallmann syndrome with associated anosmia, or acquired through pituitary or hypothalamic lesions, systemic illness, or undernutrition. In hypergonadotropic hypogonadism the testes themselves fail to respond, so gonadotropins rise, as seen in Klinefelter syndrome and after testicular damage.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism including Kallmann syndrome
Acquired hypothalamic-pituitary disease such as a tumour or infiltrative disorder
Chronic systemic illness, malnutrition, or excessive exercise suppressing the axis
Primary testicular failure including Klinefelter syndrome
Hypothyroidism and other endocrinopathies delaying maturation
additionalInvestigations: Growth assessment with height, weight, growth velocity, and pubertal (Tanner) staging including testicular volume
Bone age radiograph of the hand and wrist to gauge skeletal maturity and growth potential
Serum luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and testosterone to localise the level of the defect
Prolactin and thyroid function, with pituitary imaging when a central lesion is suspected
Karyotype where primary gonadal failure such as Klinefelter syndrome is considered
Assessment of smell and screening for associated anomalies if Kallmann syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Neurological signs, visual field loss, or headache suggesting an intracranial or pituitary lesion
Raised gonadotropins with small firm testes indicating primary gonadal failure
Features of a chronic systemic illness or significant undernutrition
Absent sense of smell with pubertal failure suggesting Kallmann syndrome
reference.prognosis: Constitutional delay carries an excellent outlook with spontaneous progression to normal adult development and fertility, whereas permanent hypogonadotropic or primary hypogonadism requires long-term hormone treatment and specific measures to achieve fertility.
pitfalls: Assuming all delay is constitutional and missing an underlying pituitary tumour or systemic disease
Failing to measure testicular volume, the key sign that puberty has begun
Overlooking anosmia, the clue to Kallmann syndrome, in a boy with low gonadotropins
Not arranging a karyotype in a boy with small firm testes and raised gonadotropins
Prolonged unnecessary hormone treatment when simple reassurance and observation would suffice
references: European Society of Endocrinology guidance on hypogonadism
management: Reassurance and monitoring in constitutional delay of growth and puberty, a benign familial variant that proceeds to full normal maturation
Short course of low-dose testosterone to induce virilisation and accelerate growth where delay causes psychological distress
Long-term testosterone replacement for permanent hypogonadotrophic or primary hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism to establish and maintain secondary sexual characteristics
Treat reversible and functional causes by optimising nutrition, managing chronic systemic illness, and correcting hyperprolactinaemia or pituitary lesions
Fertility induction with gonadotrophins or pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone in hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism when fertility is sought
Monitor growth velocity, bone age, testicular development and bone health
Karyotype and genetic counselling for Klinefelter syndrome, assessment for Kallmann syndrome including smell testing and associated anomalies, with specialist andrology or endocrinology referral
